documents.abstract: The future of modern farming is intelligent, autonomous and data-driven farming operations. This will help to address the increasing labor shortage, resource constraints and climate variability. But for deployment in unstructured agricultural settings, high-performance automation is needed, as well as trustworthy systems that can make safe decisions, have the ability to learn adaptively and collaborate effectively with human operators. In this review, we discuss recent progress in trustworthy agricultural autonomy from the perspective of three interrelated pillars: robot learning and perception, safe control and resilient planning, and human-robot interaction. This review surveys state-of-the-art perception technologies such as computer vision, LiDAR, sensor fusion and deep reinforcement learning and safety-oriented approaches including model predictive control, formal verification, failure management and resilient navigation. It also addresses human-robot collaborative systems, explainable AI, ergonomics safety and sustainability-aware robotic design and discusses ethical, regulatory and socio-economic issues related to autonomous farming. Commercial applications of autonomous weeding, robotic harvesting and broad-acre field operations are now in existence, providing real-world demonstrations of the use of these technologies, and their potential to increase productivity, improve resource efficiency and enhance environmental sustainability. Finally, the review wraps up by underlining some future research priorities like universal safety certification, edge computing, interoperability, swarm robotics, and digital twin integration. Collectively, the reviewed evidence identifies the technical, human, and governance requirements that must be addressed to support safer, more resilient, transparent, and sustainable deployment of autonomous agricultural systems. Abstract An engaging and cost-effective digital tool for developing subject-matter knowledge (SMK) could mitigate educational inequities in resource-constrained contexts. This case study explores the effectiveness of free generative artificial intelligence (GAI) platforms, prompted to function as a Flipped-Interaction Intelligent Tutoring System (FIITS), to promote science student-teacher SMK learning. Data were collected across a 10-week intervention from 42 third- and fourth-year natural and physical sciences student teachers at two campuses of a South African university. The students engaged with the FIITS in odd-numbered weeks by pasting a provided prompt into a free GAI platform, and with benchmarking interactive electronic worksheets in even-numbered weeks. Affective, behavioural, and cognitive engagement and perceptions of SMK learning were analysed using post-session questionnaires, end-of-module reflections, and group interviews. Both modalities elicited consistently high and comparable engagement levels, but students reported stronger perceptions of SMK development with the FIITS. They valued its personalisation, relevance, and human-like interactivity, although workload pressures and occasional GAI errors somewhat hindered the FIITS’s effectiveness. These findings suggest that free GAI platforms, prompted to behave as FIITS, may provide equitable, scalable, and pedagogically effective tools for improving SMK in student-teacher education. Recommendations include scaffolding an initial adjustment phase, incorporating varied levels of challenge, and managing novelty and workload to sustain engagement. This study offers early evidence of the pedagogical potential of free flipped-interaction GAI in science teacher education, particularly in contexts where access to costly educational technologies is limited.

documents.abstract: Generative AI tools promise to expand student agency in management education, yet the same tool can help and hurt learning inside a single classroom. We argue this contradiction is the signature of two psychological pathways running in parallel. Drawing on the cognitive-affective-conative framework, we develop a dual-pathway serial mediation model in which a cognitive pathway runs from psychological reactance through autonomy perceptions to effectiveness judgments, while an affective pathway runs from ethical perceptions through emotional engagement to effectiveness judgments. Ninety-seven undergraduate management students participated in two AI-enhanced activities with different chatbot tools across one semester. Both pathways operated as predicted. More surprising was how the cognitive pathway changed across exposures. At first use, reactance traveled through autonomy, consistent with self-determination theory. By the second activity, reactance bypassed autonomy and suppressed effectiveness directly. The affective pathway remained stable across exposures. For management educators, ethical framing before a student's first AI encounter may do more work than redesigning the tools themselves to preserve student choice. As a single-cohort study using two researcher-built chatbots, the results are preliminary and point to hypotheses for multi-site replication rather than population estimates.

documents.abstract: The rapid adaptation of future specialists to extreme conditions of professional activity highlights the relevance of introducing interactive simulations for realistic modeling of scenario-oriented didactic situations. The study assesses the pedagogical effectiveness of interactive simulation training in developing decision-making, situational awareness, and team interaction skills among cadets. The following methods were used for this purpose: focused search, comparative analysis, and effectiveness assessment. Empirical verification based on a sample of 64 cadets showed a significant improvement in the development dynamics of key indicators of professional training in the experimental group. The integral time of task completion decreased by 54%, the speed of cognitive reaction increased by 67%, and the accuracy of target actions (error minimization) increased by 46%. This study demonstrates a novel comprehensive pedagogical analysis of interactive simulations based on technical and functional characteristics and the integral parameter of readiness. Further research should focus on expanding the sample of participants to increase the statistical reliability of the results, as well as on analyzing a wider range of interactive technologies to determine their effectiveness in various professional scenarios.

documents.abstract: Contemporary society faces the ubiquitous proliferation of algorithmic systems that structure social life, from intimate subjective modulation to planetary crisis management. This conceptual paper therefore proposes the analytical category of vigitalization. Rooted in relational sociology, vigitalization is defined as a co-constitutive sociotechnical configuration that fuses datafication with structural surveillance to interpret the autonomization of algorithmic governance. Employing a multilevel theoretical framework bridging the macro (systematicity), meso (grouping), and micro (interaction) dimensions, the study dissects the relational interdependencies between technological infrastructures, political economy, and algocratic bureaucracies. Vigitalization operates under a strict recursive logic: digitizing to monitor and monitoring to digitize, naturalizing behavioral extraction across all institutional boundaries. Crucially, this framework positions vigitalization as the primary sociotechnical matrix governing the ASAM Nexus (Agency-Structure-Algorithm-Matter). By doing so, it equips sociology with the critical apparatus required to address the existential macro-risks, biopolitical subsumption, and biometric enclosures intrinsic to the Digital Anthropocene.

documents.abstract: Abstract: This study investigates the evolving role of Virtual Learning Environments (VLEs) in organizational training. We use PRISMA approach to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) to investigate the importance of VLE. It compiles study findings on VLEs, e-learning, and organizational learning. Training environments, learning criteria, professional training techniques, and training results are the major themes identified in this article. The study highlights challenges and opportunities associated with VLE implementation. It contributes to the discourse on workplace learning, underscoring the pivotal role of VLEs in enhancing organizational performance and employee development. Results underscore the increasing focus that businesses are placing on VLEs, stressing advantages and tackling implementation related obstacles, and extensive examination of VLE adoption. The research advances knowledge about how businesses can successfully integrate VLE procedures. The authors conclude emphasizing the strategic benefits of VLEs, suggesting avenues how businesses can successfully integrate VLE. This research is confined to the boundaries of employee performance and satisfaction. documents.abstract: With the continuous advancement of digital transformation, digital technologies such as big data and artificial intelligence have greatly reshaped corporate office practices. While these technologies significantly improve organizational work efficiency, they also produce digital hindrance stressors, which bring negative effects on employees’ mental states and work behaviors. In digital office settings, employees are faced with growing digital‑related work pressure, and cyberloafing as a type of work‑deviant behavior occurs more frequently. Drawing on self‑regulation theory, this study selects self‑regulation impairment as the mediating variable and self‑regulation trait as the moderating variable. It systematically analyzes the underlying influence path through which digital hindrance stressors act on employees’ cyberloafing behavior via self‑regulation impairment, under the moderating effect of self‑regulation trait.

DOI : https://doi.org/10.82471/qem0g-t6g81 This paper explores the emotional dependence on algorithmic feeds in the everyday social media use. Using qualitative data from a phenomenological study of internet users in Kerala, this research analyses how users experience and make sense of algorithmic recommendations in their everyday emotional contexts. The study goes beyond the usual questions on algorithmic awareness or technical understanding. It looks at how individual feeds become relevant through moods, rituals, vulnerabilities and everyday interpretations. It implies that users’ interactions with algorithms are not only shaped by visibility but also by affective experiences. The research claims that emotional dependence on algorithms is not an issue of overuse, but rather a negotiated interaction between algorithmic personalisation and user affective interpretations, foregrounding user narratives. Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are now widely applied across different domains. As AI systems increasingly shape professional and academic domains, there is a growing need to pre-pare future professionals to work with these technologies responsibly and effectively. Accordingly, an increasing number of studies advocate AI education for undergraduates across disciplines. However, there is limited qualitative research on these students’ motivations for learning about AI and on what they are interested in learning, despite the importance of such understanding for designing motivating, engaging, and effective learning experiences. Therefore, the objective of this research is to answer the following two research questions: (1) What motivates undergraduates across disciplines to learn about AI? (2) What are undergraduates across disciplines interested in learning about AI? To answer the research questions, we conducted a survey with 128 students who voluntarily enrolled in an elective introductory AI course over three semesters. The findings indicate that these students are motivated to learn about AI not only for career-related utility but also due to its perceived societal relevance and ethical implications. Regarding learning interests, students most frequently expressed interest in learning how AI systems work, how these systems impact society positively and negatively, and how to use them effectively and responsibly. In the discussion section, we provide guidance on how these results can inform the design or adaptation of AI curricula, course invitations, and learning experiences to foster sustained engagement and meaningful learning among these students.

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how constructive alignment, context support, psychological safety and defensive routines are associated with observable indicators of workplace learning in civil-military crisis exercises and why exercise participation should not be equated with demonstrated learning. Design/methodology/approach This study is a comparative qualitative reanalysis of two previously studied Swedish exercise settings conducted between 2022 and 2024. No new empirical data was collected for this study. The structurally nonequivalent cases are compared using the same deductive workplace-learning framework; the comparison is used to elaborate theory rather than to estimate causal effects. Findings Case A exhibited more observable indicators of learning progression, along with clearer objectives, sequenced activities, feedback opportunities and stronger contextual support. Case B displayed fewer such indicators alongside vague objectives, limited assessment, heterogeneous participant experience and recurring defensive routines. Because the cases also differ in duration, immersion, group stability, participant composition and unit of analysis, these patterns are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects of exercise design. Research limitations/implications The comparison concerns one five-day exercise and a composite of seven exercises, uses unequal qualitative corpora and lacks independent pre- and postmeasures or behavioral evidence of transfer. This study therefore identifies theoretically relevant patterns and observable learning-process indicators, not verified individual learning outcomes or causal effects. Practical implications Exercise planners should connect specific learning objectives to role-relevant activities and structured feedback, while deliberately providing legal expertise, role clarity, facilitation and conditions for speaking up. Evaluation should distinguish immediate exercise outputs from subsequent transfer to ordinary work. Originality/value This study does not add new empirical data. Its contribution is a standardized cross-case reanalysis that integrates constructive alignment with workplace-learning affordances, psychological safety, defensive routines and training-transfer research and specifies the boundary conditions under which exercise outputs can be interpreted as indicators of learning progression.

documents.abstract: People are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, and those agents are increasingly encountering other people's agents over shared resources such as a codebase, a calendar, or a budget. When each agent acts for a different user with different goals, coordination often fails, and the group ends up worse off than if a single agent had acted for everyone. We study this multi-user, multi-agent setting across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments: an API key environment in which agents share a compute budget, a clinic in which they share a calendar, a personal assistant environment in which they share a group order or booking, and a merge queue in which they share a release cutoff. In each scenario, we compare a single agent that serves every user (a coordinator) to a team in which each agent serves one user, with and without a communication channel between the agents. Teams deliver worse group outcomes than the coordinator in every environment: without a channel, they completely collapse in two environments, and even with one, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps. For example, in the personal assistant environment, the coordinator fulfills a targeted user request about twice as often as teams. We identify distinct behaviors associated with this poor group-level performance, including stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, and fabricating claims. We find effective but environment-specific mitigations, such as a team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and a platform check that makes an agent read its peers' messages before committing. We will release the API key, clinic, and personal assistant environments as MAMUBench, comprising 74 scenarios for evaluating multi-user, multi-agent coordination.

Generative AI (GenAI) has revolutionized academic writing, shifting the nature of human-AI interactions in text production. While previous studies focus on academic honesty and general writing outcomes, little research addresses how multilingual university students negotiate authorial identities during AI integration. This qualitative study explores the negotiation of authorial identity among 15 postgraduate students at Mahendra Multiple Campus, Tribhuvan University, Nepal, using semi-structured interviews and reflexive thematic analysis. Guided by Ivanič’s Writer Identity Theory, Vygotsky’s Sociocultural Theory, Norton’s Identity and Investment Theory, and Bourdieu’s Linguistic Capital Theory, the study investigates students' perceptions of authorship, creativity, and linguistic voice. Empirically, the findings reveal five key outcomes: (1) students utilize GenAI primarily as a linguistic scaffolding tool to bridge conceptual ideas and formal academic English; (2) authorship is experienced as a negotiated sociotechnical space where intellectual ownership of ideas remains human while linguistic expression is co-constructed; (3) GenAI acts as a cognitive and creative partner that stimulates alternative argumentation rather than replacing human ingenuity; (4) participants experience an internal tension between achieving polished Western-centric academic English and preserving their authentic multilingual voices; and (5) sustainable writing relies on robust human agency, critical evaluation, and editorial oversight. These findings demonstrate that AI is not a mere substitution tool but an intervening mediator that reshapes scholarly writing. The study offers critical insights from a South Asian multilingual higher education context, advocating for AI-literate classrooms that foster intellectual ownership while enabling responsible technological utilization.

The article substantiates the concept of national resilience as an emerging governance paradigm within Ukraine's state security system. Drawing on an analysis of NATO, EU, and International Organization for Standardization standards, as well as Ukrainian strategic documents, the study elucidates the distinctions between the traditional "security" paradigm and the dynamic paradigm of "resilience". The paper proposes institutional mechanisms for interagency coordination, algorithms for establishing unified situational awareness, and protocols for subsidiarity-based response and public-private partnership. It is demonstrated that resilience functions as an integrated framework for managing challenges and threats under conditions of hybrid warfare. The scientific novelty lies in the development of a matrix model for coordinating security actors that incorporates a network-centric approach into public administration. The practical significance is reflected in the applicability of the proposed mechanisms for assessing the resilience levels of public administration sectors, critical infrastructure, and cybersecurity.

The article presents the results of a study addressing the challenges associated with organizing and maintaining interoperability between units of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine (SBGSU) and other components of the Defense Forces of Ukraine under the conditions of full-scale armed aggression. Based on an analysis of existing scientific and methodological materials, as well as operational and combat experience gained during 2022–2025, practical recommendations are proposed for implementing the modular organizational framework and integrating automated situational awareness systems (the Delta system) into this framework. These measures are considered key factors in achieving the required levels of adequacy and responsiveness in organizing interoperability among SBGSU forces and assets while performing missions as part of the Defense Forces under martial law.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to examine the current situation, problems, and needs for standard development; develop and evaluate operating standards; and establish the 2025 Situation Awareness Team Operating Standards of the Department of Disease Control. This action research was conducted from January 2025 to February 2026 and comprised five phases: (1) reviewing relevant documents and standards; (2) developing draft standards; (3) pilot testing in three Offices of Disease Prevention and Control; (4) revising the standards based on pilot test findings and expert recommendations; and (5) finalizing the standards. Results: The 2025 Situation Awareness Team Operating Standards of the Department of Disease Control comprised six domains: team establishment, technical capacity, operational readiness, surveillance and situation assessment, quality of outbreak reports, and supporting systems, monitoring, and evaluation. Pilot implementation demonstrated that the participating agencies were able to use the standards for self-assessment. The indicators were clear, reflected actual practice, and helped identify gaps for strengthening the situation awareness system.

documents.abstract: While AI is often viewed as a strategic resource for improving efficiency and competitiveness, its outcomes remain uneven across organizations. Limited conceptual clarity remains regarding how artificial intelligence adoption contributes to organizational resilience, particularly in turbulent South Asian contexts. This paper argues that the missing link lies in AI readiness, conceptualized as a multidimensional capability that reflects the extent to which organizations and their employees are prepared to adopt, use, and adapt to AI technologies. Based on an integrative review, the study draws on the Resource-Based View, dynamic capabilities theory, and leadership perspectives to develop a conceptual framework that positions AI readiness as a mediating mechanism between leadership and organizational resilience. Leadership is conceptualized as an enabling force that shapes organizational conditions and supports capability development, while AI readiness facilitates the translation of technological potential into adaptive capacity. Organizational resilience is viewed as a dynamic capability involving anticipation, coping, and adaptation under disruption. The study further situates this framework within the context of South Asian economies characterized by institutional volatility, resource constraints, and uneven digital maturity. It argues that under such conditions, leadership-enabled AI readiness becomes particularly critical for sustaining organizational performance. The paper contributes to theory by integrating leadership, AI readiness, and resilience within a capability-based framework and offers practical insights for organizations seeking to navigate technological change in turbulent environments.

documents.abstract: Decision making in business-to-consumer (B2C) e-commerce connects company and consumer activities before, during and after purchase. Existing generative artificial intelligence (GAI) applications usually address isolated tasks. This article develops a conceptual framework in which the five-stage Consumer Buying Behaviour (CBB) process structures GAI-assisted decisions. It links need clarification, information gathering, feasible-offer comparison, transaction review and post-purchase assessment in a recursive cycle with decision gates and bounded support functions. To illustrate its measurement and reporting procedure, five employees and three consumers completed baseline tasks followed by intended-to-be-comparable prompt-guided cases. No integrated GAI system, autonomous agent, live data connection or consequential transaction was implemented. The questionnaire items are descriptive indicators, not validated latent constructs, and findings are limited to participant-specific summaries. Several rubric-based and self-reported values were numerically more favourable in the second condition, but the fixed order prevents separation of prompt support from practice, familiarity, novelty, fatigue or expectancy effects. Technical accuracy, trust calibration, automation bias, commercial impact and post-purchase outcomes were not evaluated. The pilot is a procedural illustration and design input; it does not validate the framework or establish effectiveness. Larger randomized or counterbalanced studies using validated measures, task-level records and implemented-system tests are required.

This article develops a philosophical-conceptual framework for rethinking Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence (HCAI) through the pragmatic semiotics of Charles Sanders Peirce. Rather than treating explainability solely as algorithmic transparency, the article conceptualizes it as a socially situated epistemic process through which AI-generated outputs are interpreted, evaluated, contested, and revised within human practices of inquiry. Drawing on Peirce’s concepts of semiosis, abduction, inquiry, fallibilism, pragmaticism, and the community of inquiry, the framework distinguishes between computational processes performed by AI systems and the human and institutional practices through which their outputs acquire epistemic and practical significance. AI outputs may function as signs and may generate hypotheses that are functionally analogous to abductive possibilities; however, interpretation, evidential assessment, justification, ethical judgment, and responsibility remain situated within human communities of inquiry. The framework further translates Peircean concepts into practical principles for XAI, including contextual interpretation, uncertainty communication, contestability, human review, stakeholder participation, evidence-based revision, and continuous evaluation. A worked example involving generative AI illustrates how an AI-generated explanation can move through interpretation, questioning, evidence checking, contestation, and revision rather than being accepted as a final epistemic product. The article therefore positions Peircean pragmatism not as a replacement for technical XAI methods but as a philosophical and normative framework that complements them by clarifying the epistemological conditions of meaningful explanation, trustworthy human oversight, and responsible AI governance.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This study addresses a persistent challenge in community resilience research and practice: how to assess and build resilience when communities face multiple, interacting, and potentially unforeseen risks. It develops a relational framework for multi‐risk resilience based on Person–Environment (P–E) Fit Theory. The study conceptualizes community resilience as emerging at the intersection of three interrelated determinants: Knowledge about self and the environment, Assets (natural, built, social) in the environment, and Support Services that address gaps between Knowledge and Assets. Risk and vulnerability arise or intensify where relationships among Knowledge, Assets and Support Services are poorly aligned, while resilience is strengthened through their mutually reinforcing alignment. One‐Risk concept is introduced in this study as providing a common relational layer for examining how this alingnment conditions different risk configurations. The framework is operationalized through SCORE (Stakeholder Co‐Creation and Review), an original co‐creation methodology simulating co‐creative resilience and combining stakeholder agency, peer review, quantitative agreement thresholding, and defined decision rights. Six stakeholders representing different sectors and multi‐risk contexts across the UK, India, USA, China, and South Africa initially proposed 54 interrelating indicators under the three determinants. Following peer review and an 80% agreement threshold for retention, 24 indicators were retained: five Knowledge (e.g., situation awareness index), 13 Assets (e.g., protective nature index), and six Support Services (e.g., resilience planning index) indicators. Each indicator is accompanied by a measurement metric and provisional vulnerability threshold. Their main contribution lies in their relational organization through the One‐Risk framework to reveal potential P‐E mismatches and support the development of relational resilience profiles. The resulting framework encourages a shift from asking whether a community possesses sufficient resilience attributes to asking where mismatches between community abilities, environmental conditions, and support services generate vulnerability, and which mutually reinforcing interventions can reduce those mismatches across multiple risk configurations. This is the principal basis on which this study extends the existing literature on multi‐risk resilience.

This policy framework sets out the values, principles, and human rights that should govern research assessment as data and artificial intelligence change both the research being assessed and the means of assessing it. It is deliverable 2.1 of Workstream 2 of CoARA-ERIP. The framework grounds research assessment in the human right to science and the rights connected with it, names six values that the CoARA-ERIP community holds in common, and derives from them twelve principles, among them human judgement, evidence mapping in place of ranking, contestability, the recognition of a plurality of contributions, and the openness of research information. It identifies the commitments that fall to research-performing organisations, research-funding organisations, evaluators, researchers, infrastructure providers, and policymakers; distinguishes uses of artificial intelligence in assessment that may be supported, that require particular care, and that are not appropriate; and sets out how the framework is implemented, monitored, and reviewed. The companion deliverables, the framework for assessing digital contributions (2.2) and the methodological guidelines (2.3), carry the framework into method and instruments.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming educational landscapes worldwide, with applications ranging from intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive learning platforms to automated assessment and personalized feedback mechanisms. In physics education specifically, AI-supported tools have demonstrated potential to enhance conceptual understanding, problem-solving skills, and student engagement by providing individualized learning pathways and real-time diagnostic feedback. However, the integration of AI in education remains highly uneven across global contexts. While developed countries possess the infrastructure, resources, and institutional capacity to implement AI-supported learning at scale, developing countries face persistent challenges including limited digital infrastructure, inadequate teacher training, and constrained educational budgets. The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated these disparities, revealing profound gaps in educational technology access and preparedness. SDG 4 (Quality Education) calls for ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and promoting lifelong learning opportunities for all. Target 4.4 specifically emphasizes increasing the number of youth and adults with relevant skills, including ICT skills . SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) aims to reduce inequality within and among countries, with Target 10.2 emphasizing the social, economic, and political inclusion of all . The intersection of AI-supported physics education and these two SDGs represents a critical yet underexplored research area. While AI has the potential to democratize access to high-quality physics instruction—particularly in regions facing teacher shortages—it may also exacerbate existing inequalities if deployment is uneven or culturally inappropriate. A systematic synthesis of existing evidence is necessary to understand what works, for whom, and under what conditions. This review addresses a significant gap: no comprehensive systematic review currently exists that synthesizes evidence on AI-supported physics education specifically in developing country contexts with explicit attention to equity and inclusion outcomes.
